title: Investigating a hemagglutinin mediated molecular mechanism of avian influenza A virus host tropism
text:
With the use of smFRET and a bulk fusion assay, this application proposes to (1), characterize the early
dynamic events of pH-triggered conformational changes of influenza A virus (IAV) hemagglutinin (HA) and (2),
characterize the extent to which the regulation of the pre- to post-fusion conformational change is different
between avian HA serotypes and human adapted serotypes. These experiments will lead to a better
understanding of fusion mechanism of HA but will also reveal differences in the regulation between avian HA
serotypes and human adapted serotypes. Identifying differences in the regulation of avian HA and human HA
will help build a mechanism to describe the host tropism of IAV with the goal of improving genetic surveillance
to identify variants of concern.

title: Passive immunotherapy for measles infection
text:
Measles (MeV) causes a severe transient immunosuppression in healthy individual and can cause lethal
encephalitis in immunocompromised people. For these people vaccination is not an option and the only
intervention in case of exposure is hyperimmune sera obtained from vaccinated individuals. Recent advances
in our MeV research are ready to be applied to developing a new passive immunotherapy that will lead to a
highly effective cocktail of long-lasting neutralizing antibodies.

title: FX ENTRAIN: Perturbation of neurodynamics underlying sensory hyperarousal and statistical learning in Youth with FXS
text:
Contact PI/PD: Pedapati, Ernest
NARRATIVE
Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) is a leading cause of inherited autism and intellectual disability, and despite a
tremendous body of multi-species translational and clinical investigation, breakthroughs in treatments have not
been forthcoming. We seek to address two major causes of this discrepancy by a systematic study of the basis
of individual heterogeneity and higher-level cognitive symptomatology through the application of novel
analytics of transient, non-continuous events and computation modeling of empirical data and implementation
of a double-blind, individualized closed-loop auditory entrainment perturbation study to isolate neural targets
associated with sensory hyperarousal and statistical learning.

title: Modulation of Olfactory Processing by Glucagon-like Peptide 1 Signaling
text: GLP-1-based therapies are frontline treatments for obesity and type 2 diabetes, yet the mechanisms by which GLP-1 influences sensory perception and food motivation remain poorly understood. This project will reveal how central GLP-1 signaling regulates olfactory sensory representations and sensory-driven behavior, and how diet-induced obesity perturbs these processes. These findings may uncover a new mechanism by which metabolic state reshapes olfactory function, offering broader insight into how obesity alters the neural control of feeding.

title: The role of the subacromial bursa in rotator cuff degeneration and healing
text:
Rotator cuff disease is a significant clinical problem affecting millions of individuals each year. Rotator cuff tears
require repair of tendon to bone, yet successful healing is rarely achieved. Our aim is to translate our recent
discoveries on the role of the bursa in rotator cuff healing into treatments for improving outcomes after rotator
cuff repair.

title: Inhibition of lipoprotein synthesis in Helicobacter pylori
text:
(Relevance to Public Health) Helicobacter pylori can be eradicated from the stomach,
reducing the incidence of diseases including ulcers and gastric cancer. However, increasing antibiotic resistance
among H. pylori strains is reducing the effectiveness of current treatment regimens. A long-term goal of this
research is the development of new therapeutics to treat H. pylori infection.

title: Study of PTPRF-Mediated Regulation of Wnt Signaling
text:
Wnt signaling is a rapidly evolving and important field of investigation and new regulators involved in this
cascade are continuously being identified. Our study focuses on developing a mechanistic understanding of
PTPRF-mediated regulation of Wnt signaling and intestinal stem cell function. Results from our studies will help
identify new therapeutic strategies for treating Wnt-driven diseases by using PTPRF as a target.

title: Tuberculosis Bioinformatics Training Program
text: The Tuberculosis Bioinformatics Training Program aims to strengthen bioinformatics training for infectious dis-eases, specifically for tuberculosis (TB), a major public health problem whose incidence in the US is increasing by 16% annually. The Program will address a shortage of skilled bioinformaticians with expertise in TB and other infectious diseases, through a structured Master’s in TB bioinformatics, in which trainees will develop subject-specific expertise, complemented by international research visits, and other networking and capacity development opportunities. Trainees will be embedded within a vibrant network of International and US-based mentors, equipping them to become leaders in global infectious disease bioinformatics, while contributing high-quality, reproducible data to the US scientific enterprise from an international setting where studying TB in hu-man populations is less expensive and more data rich, due to its high prevalence.

title: timsTOF HT for High Throughput Proteomics
text: This proposal requests funding to procure a Bruker timsTOF HT mass spectrometer to be housed and operated at the Stanford University Mass Spectrometry shared resource laboratory. The instrument will be tasked with meeting the high throughput demands of our NIH-funded researchers on campus, covering a diverse panoply of proteomics research topics which require an instrument platform capable of providing sufficient data to draw biomedical implications from clinical and similarly large-scale research projects. In this role the instrument will support the NIH’s many missions and accelerate currently structured research projects in a multitude of areas, including but not limited to cellular regulation, synaptic vesicle formation and release, heart disease, ocular inflammation, infectious disease, and cancer treatment and response.

title: Rehabilitation Technology
text: 7. Project Summary: RC-3 The Rehabilitation Technology Resource Core (RC-3) supports the UM-OAIC mission by advancing scientific, technological, and translational research in rehabilitation for older adults. RC-3 provides investigators with specialized expertise in neuromotor, musculoskeletal, and cognitive assessment and intervention, facilitating the development, validation, and implementation of evidence-based rehabilitation technologies. The core operates through an integrated framework encompassing mechanistic discovery, technology validation, and real-world integration, with active stakeholder engagement (clinicians, industry partners, older adults, patient advisory groups) at every stage. RC-3 is co-led by Drs. Li-Qun Zhang (bioengineering, rehabilitation robotics, neuroplastic facilitation) and Kelly Westlake (motor learning, brain imaging, fall prevention), supported by multidisciplinary investigators with expertise spanning biomechanics, neuropsychology, neuroimaging, and clinical rehabilitation. The core leverages specialized facilities including the Neuromechanics Lab, NeuMo Lab, UM Rehabilitation & Orthopaedic Institute, Center for Translational Research in Imaging, and the new St. John Center for Translational Engineering and Medicine. Major innovations include FDA-approved lower limb robotics (AMBLE), Off-axis stepping trainer, novel upper limb devices (REACH robot, IntelliArm multi-joint robot, GENESIS II FES), wearable assessment systems (GAIT device), portable balance assessment tools (MOBAL), and AI-enhanced fall-risk profiling platforms. These technologies have emerged through iterative industry partnerships with NextStep Robotics, Rehabtek, and Restorative Therapies, supported by >$14M in extramural funding and resulting in 51 publications during the previous cycle. Specific Aim 1 advances mechanistic discovery in neuromotor, musculoskeletal, and cognitive domains through integrated multidomain assessments (biomechanical, brain imaging, cognitive, psychophysiological) to define precision rehabilitation targets. Specific Aim 2 accelerates development, validation, and implementation readiness of mechanistically informed technologies through device optimization, multi-domain outcome assessment, clinical trial infrastructure, and regulatory guidance across laboratory, clinic, and community settings. Specific Aim 3 fosters investigator success through cross-core collaboration, tailored mentorship, and multidisciplinary consultation, prioritizing REC Scholars, pilot awardees, and early career investigators. RC-3 integrates tightly with RC-1 (data science, machine learning applications) and RC-2 (molecular/physiological discoveries translated into interventions), while establishing cross-OAIC collaborations and a proposed Technology Dissemination Network. The core provides comprehensive services spanning accurate assessment of impairment, technology validation, stakeholder engagement, clinical trial support, and commercialization guidance, facilitating technologies for regulatory clearance and real-world impact on older adult function and independence.

title: New Tools and Approaches for Understanding Metal-Mediated Interactions in the Extracellular Space
text:
The proposed research seeks to develop and apply analytical and sensing tools for understanding
bioavailable metals in the extracellular environment with a focus on blood-based fluids.
Incorporated in this work is the study of how metals may facilitate the trafficking and signaling of
peptide hormones. Insight from these investigations will be help identify new biomarkers and
inform peptide-based therapeutic development in diseases like diabetes, liver disease, and
cardiovascular disorders.

title: Chromatin regulation of epithelial stem cell function
text:
Dedicated adult stem cells play an important role in renewing epithelial tissues during homeostasis, but their
regenerative function can also be supported following injury by mature cells that dedifferentiate and exhibit
“facultative” stem cell function. Over the next five years, this project will examine how genetic regulatory
programs control dedicated (or ”active”) and transient (“facultative”) stem cells, with the overarching goal of
understanding how these programs vary between cell populations and sources of injury. These studies will
advance our basic understanding of tissue renewal, regeneration, and long-term impacts of injury with
fundamental relevance to human health and disease, including traumatic injury, inflammation, aging, and cancer.

title: Cell and Tissue Imaging (CTI)
text: The Cell and Tissue Imaging Shared Resource (CTI-SR), is a centralized, shared instrumentation resource with advanced microscopy and imaging technologies that are vital to studying cell and tissue morphology and ultrastructure. As such, the facility provides a cost-effective solution for Rogel researchers to utilize state-ofthe-art imaging instrumentation with the technical support necessary to succeed in both routine and advanced imaging modalities from inception to publication. In addition to offering instrument time, CTI-SR offers routine and advanced services in electron microscopy sample processing, sectioning, staining, and analysis. The availability of highly trained personnel with years of expertise is a distinct advantage to Rogel members, as is the Rogel member subsidy. The facility also emphasizes training to ensure that all users operate the advanced equipment properly, independent of prior experience.

title: Microscopy, Imaging and Cytometry Resources (MICR)
text: The purpose of the Microscopy, Imaging and Cytometry Resources (MICR) Core is to enhance the peer reviewed funded research activities of KCI members whose research requires confocal microscopy, flow cytometry, small animal imaging and related techniques. To this end, during the current funding period, the Core has contributed to 115 peer reviewed publications by Cancer Center members, representing a 25% increase over the previous submission. Capabilities and services include: confocal microscopy, multiphoton microscopy, conventional light microscopy, FRET and FRAP, TIRF and Atomic Force Microscopy, in vivo animal imaging (including SPECT, CT, PET, x-ray, and optical imaging), flow cytometry and radiometric analyses (e.g., intracellular pH and ion measurement studies), as well as three- and four-dimensional image reconstruction and quantitative measurements. MR imaging is also available through a collaborative effort between MICR and the WSU MR Center. Our advanced instrumentation consists of 1: seven confocal microscopes including (a Zeiss LSM 410 confocal microscope equipped with six laser lines, a Zeiss Cell Observer spinning disk confocal microscope equipped with three laser lines, a Zeiss LSM-510 META NLO confocal microscope with eight laser lines and multiphoton imaging, a Leica TCS-SP5 MP equipped with nine laser lines and multiphoton capability, a newly acquired Olympus/Bruker TIRF/AFM custom microscope, cutting-edge Zeiss LSM 780 confocal microscope with six conventional laser lines and the InTune laser, a tunable white light laser with over 200 laser lines, a Zeiss LSM 800 with four lasers and the super-resolution Airyscan detector and a Leica SP8 confocal microscope with 4 lasers); 2: three conventional fluorescent microscopes (two with the state-of-the-art Apotome module capable of four dimensional imaging); 3: six flow cytometers (including a Becton Dickinson (BD) LSR II, a BD FACSCanto II, a Sony SY3200 cell sorter, two Sony SH800 sorter analyzers, and the Amnis ImageStreamX Mark II imaging flow cytometer). 4: six in vivo animal imagers (including Bruker In Vivo Extreme and MS FX Pro small animal optical/x-ray imagers, a Siemens Inveon SPECT/CT, Concord Focus 220 microPET, Bruker Albira small animal PET/CT scanner and a GE Discovery LS4 clinical PET/CT scanner for large animal imaging). As mentioned above, small animal MRI is also available through collaborative efforts between MICR and the MR Center located next door. The analytical systems of the MICR Core include eight Apple and PC workstations with various analytical software and photographic quality printers and the MIP, Molecular Imaging Portal. MIP is a UNIX based central server with 45 TB storage capacity and a 74 TB robotic tape backup system as well as a dedicated applications server hosting the advance image analysis software, Matlab™ and Definiens™, with two licenses each allowing up to two users access to each software simultaneously.

title: Assessment of Twin Gestation with AI-Assisted Ultrasound
text:
Twin pregnancy is risky to both mother and babies. This proposal aims to develop a suite of AI-enabled
ultrasound tools to improve the diagnosis and management of twins.

title: Tachycardia-induced Metabolic Remodeling Drives Cardiac Dysfunction
text:
Tachycardia, or abnormally fast heart rate, is an independent risk factor for adverse cardiovascular events and
it is known to induce or exacerbate heart failure. However, the mechanistic understanding of how increased heart
rate leads to cardiac dysfunction is very limited. This proposal will capitalize on recent technological advances
in stem cell biology, tissue engineering, and multi-omics to address this gap in our knowledge, thereby opening
new opportunities for therapeutic interventions for relevant heart diseases.

title: Video Disease Activity Index: A novel video measure to monitor rheumatoid arthritis in telehealth
text:
In rheumatology practice there is an unmet need for a system that can collect accurate information on disease
activity during telehealth consultations. We will implement and validate a new technology that uses smartphone
cameras to capture visual measures of joint-specific information such as range of motion and joint swelling.
The technology can lead to faster and more precise measurement of symptoms in telehealth visits to optimize
medication and therapy interventions.

title: World Molecular Imaging Congress (WMIC)
text:
R13 Grant Narrative WMIC 2026
The WMIC 2026 will advance public health by accelerating innovation in molecular imaging technologies that
improve the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of human disease. Funding to support the participation of
graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, and early-career investigators at WMIC 2026 will expand access to
advanced scientific education, mentoring, and networking aligned with Aim 1 (active trainee engagement) and
Aim 2 (deepening understanding of disease biology and imaging science). These opportunities will strengthen
the national biomedical imaging workforce and foster the interdisciplinary collaborations essential for
translating molecular imaging discoveries into clinical impact.

title: Streptococcus species as potential therapeutics for oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma
text:
In this project, Ph.D. and B.S. students will identify oral commensal non-pathogenic Streptococcus species, such
as S. Salivarius and/or S. vestibularis, capable of decreasing cancer cell survival and modulating the tumor
immune microenvironment during oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). Students will be trained in
cancer immunology and cancer biology to achieve our long-term goal of developing microbial therapeutics for
OSCC.

title: Dissecting reciprocal interactions between cancer cells and endothelial cells in SCLC liver metastasis.
text:
Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a recalcitrant cancer that causes 250,000 deaths worldwide each
year. When diagnosed, many patients have metastasis in distant organs, most often in the liver,
which represents a major impediment to successful therapy. Through decrypting the reciprocal
interactions between cancer cells and endothelial cells in SCLC liver metastasis, I aim to identify
novel aspects of SCLC metastasis and nominate candidate avenues for target therapies for
SCLC patients.
